also.hook: Chris Olah helped invent the field of mechanistic interpretability, the effort to reverse engineer the internal workings of neural networks into algorithms a person can actually read. He built that career without a college degree, funding it instead with a Thiel Fellowship, then spent years at Google Brain visualizing what neural networks see before leading interpretability research at OpenAI. In 2021 he co-founded Anthropic and now leads its interpretability work, publishing the Transformer Circuits research thread that tries to map language models circuit by circuit. He also co-founded Distill, a journal built around explaining machine learning clearly rather than tersely. In 2026 he took that argument to the Vatican, telling an audience beside Pope Leo XIV that AI's governance problems cannot be left to computer scientists alone.
also.name: Chris Olah

also.hook: Dario Amodei trained as a physicist, earning a Ph.D. in biophysics from Princeton as a Hertz Fellow before moving into machine learning at Baidu, briefly at Google Brain, and then at OpenAI. As OpenAI's Vice President of Research, he set research direction, led the teams that built GPT-2 and GPT-3, and helped pioneer reinforcement learning from human feedback. In 2021 he left to co-found Anthropic, where as CEO he has pushed the idea that AI safety and frontier capability can be built together rather than traded off. He argues that case publicly too, from his 2024 essay Machines of Loving Grace on AI's potential upside to a 2025 New York Times op-ed calling for basic transparency rules on frontier AI development.
also.name: Dario Amodei

also.hook: Eliezer Yudkowsky is an American writer and researcher who has spent more than two decades arguing that artificial intelligence poses a serious risk to humanity's survival. Without a formal academic degree, he co-founded the Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence, later renamed the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, with Brian and Sabine Atkins in 2000 to help accelerate the arrival of smarter than human AI. Within a few years he concluded that building such systems safely was a harder and more urgent problem than building them at all, and he redirected the institute's research toward what became known as AI alignment. Between 2006 and 2012 he wrote a long series of essays on rationality, cognitive bias, and AI risk that helped found the online community LessWrong and were later collected into the book Rationality: From AI to Zombies. In 2023 he argued in a Time magazine essay that a temporary pause on AI development was not enough and called for governments to shut down large AI training runs entirely. In 2025 he co-authored If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies with fellow MIRI researcher Nate Soares, bringing his warnings about superintelligent AI to a mainstream audience.
also.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
also.moniker: AI alignment researcher and co-founder of MIRI

also.hook: Hinton kept faith with neural networks through two AI winters, and won. The training method he championed in 1986 and the 2012 breakthrough his lab produced turned a marginal idea into the technology behind modern AI. Then, at the peak of vindication, he quit Google to warn the world about what he had helped build, giving AI risk its most credentialed voice.
also.name: Geoffrey Hinton

also.hook: Yoshua Bengio has spent his career pushing neural networks from a marginal idea into the foundation of modern AI, and more recently has turned much of his attention to the risks that AI now poses. Born in Paris and raised in Canada, he earned a PhD in computer science from McGill University before joining the Universite de Montreal, where he has been a professor since the early 1990s. His 2003 paper A Neural Probabilistic Language Model helped establish the use of learned word representations in language modeling, an idea that became central to later large language models, and in 2014 he co-authored the paper introducing generative adversarial networks with Ian Goodfellow and others. He founded Mila, the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, building it into one of the world's largest academic centers for deep learning research, and in 2016 co-founded the AI startup Element AI. In 2018 he shared the ACM A.M. Turing Award with Yann LeCun and Geoffrey Hinton for his contributions to deep learning. In recent years he has chaired the International AI Safety Report and, in June 2025, launched LawZero, a nonprofit research organization focused on building safe, non-agentic AI systems.
also.name: Yoshua Bengio
also.moniker: Professor, Universite de Montreal, and founder of Mila and LawZero

profiles.hook: Dan Hendrycks holds a PhD in computer science from UC Berkeley. In 2016 he and Kevin Gimpel introduced the Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) activation function, which went on to become one of the most widely used activation functions in transformer-based neural networks, including BERT and GPT-style models. In 2020 he led a team that created the MMLU benchmark, a test spanning 57 academic and professional subjects that became a standard way to measure how much large language models actually know rather than how fluently they write. He serves as Executive and Research Director of the Center for AI Safety, a nonprofit focused on reducing societal-scale risks from artificial intelligence, and in 2023 he organized the Statement on AI Risk, a public letter signed by leading AI researchers and company executives that helped push AI extinction risk into mainstream policy debate. He also advises xAI and Scale AI and wrote the textbook Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics, and Society.

profiles.hook: Paul Christiano holds a PhD in statistical learning theory from UC Berkeley. While working on the alignment team at OpenAI, he was a co-author and principal architect of the 2017 paper Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences, which introduced the technique now known as reinforcement learning from human feedback, using human comparisons between possible outputs to train reinforcement learning systems. That approach was later adapted to fine-tune large language models and became a standard part of how systems like ChatGPT are trained to follow instructions and match human judgment. In 2021 he left OpenAI to found the Alignment Research Center (ARC), a nonprofit that develops theoretical and empirical methods for understanding and evaluating advanced AI systems, including work on eliciting latent knowledge from neural networks. He was named to the Time 100 Most Influential People in AI in 2023, and in 2024 he began advising the U.S. government's AI safety evaluation work through what is now NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation.

profiles.hook: Stuart Russell is Distinguished Professor of Computer Science at UC Berkeley, where he also holds the Smith-Zadeh Professorship in Engineering and a professorship in Cognitive Science. With Peter Norvig he co-authored Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, first published in 1995 and now in multiple editions, which became the standard textbook used to teach AI in universities worldwide. In 2016 he founded the Center for Human-Compatible AI (CHAI) at Berkeley, a research lab devoted to redesigning AI systems around explicit uncertainty about human preferences rather than fixed objectives, on the argument that optimizing a fixed goal too well is what makes highly capable AI systems dangerous. He set out that argument for a general audience in his 2019 book Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control, and in 2021 he delivered the BBC's Reith Lectures on living with artificial intelligence. He holds an OBE and is a Fellow of the Royal Society, and also serves as Professor of Computational Precision Health at UCSF and an Honorary Fellow of Wadham College, Oxford.
